query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an optimal amount of tungsten carbide (WC) into a high-entropy alloy (HEA) will form lubricious in situ carbide phases that reduce both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: An unmodified HEA matrix (e.g., FeCoCrNi-based) with a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Composition modification by adding an optimized WC content to the HEA, aiming to generate lubricious carbide phases during processing.
generation.conditions: The modified HEA will be evaluated under a broad temperature range, from room temperature up to high temperatures (e.g., 600–800 °C) representative of service conditions encountered in self-lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of dispersed carbide phases (e.g., Cr-rich carbides and Co3W3C) within the HEA matrix that act as lubricious and hard phases.
generation.mechanism: The added WC reacts during processing to form hard, lubricious carbide phases that reduce adhesion and abrasive wear. These carbides improve hardness and create a protective tribo-film that mitigates the coefficient of friction even under elevated thermal activation and cyclic loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate relative to untreated HEA, while maintaining mechanical integrity across a wide temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated HEA, which typically shows higher friction coefficients and wear rates due to its homogeneous structure lacking lubricious, reinforcing carbide phases.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only if the WC content is optimized; excessive WC may lead to poor phase bonding and increased friction. The hypothesis might not hold if processing variables do not favor proper in situ carbide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal WC content and the exact quantitative improvement in friction and wear are uncertain pending further experimental optimization, as the trade-off with potential brittleness or interface issues remains to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set modified with the optimized WC content and one unmodified control group. Process both samples using identical techniques. Conduct systematic tribological tests across a temperature range (e.g., RT to 800 °C) using a standardized sliding wear apparatus. Analyze both the friction coefficient and wear rate along with microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM and XRD) to verify the presence and distribution of the in situ-formed carbide phases.
measurements: Coefficient of friction measured via wear tests at multiple temperatures
Quantification of wear rate (e.g., volume loss, weight loss)
Microstructural analyses (SEM, XRD) to confirm formation and distribution of carbide phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WC-modified HEA does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared with the unmodified HEA across the tested temperature range, or if the expected lubricious carbide phases are absent, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. The Effect of WC Content on Properties of Composites
cited_evidence.text: The strengthening mechanisms of WC particle-reinforced HEA matrix composites mainly include the second phase strengthening of the hard phase itself, the dislocation strengthening introduced by the difference in thermal expansion coefficients between the hard phase and the matrix, the fine grain strengthening of the matrix grains by the hard phase during the ball milling process, and solid solution strengthening caused by diffusion of W and C atoms [,].

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. The Effect of WC Content on Properties of Composites
cited_evidence.text: WC particles have high hardness, good wear resistance, strong resistance to deformation during friction, and are less prone to plastic deformation, resulting in increased friction resistance and stronger wear resistance of the composites. With the increase of WC content, the wear mechanism of HEA matrix composites changes from adhesive wear to abrasive wear, and the formation of second phases such as Cr-rich and Co3W3C carbides in the composites also reduces the wear volume, which is beneficial to the improvement of wear resistance of HEA matrix. When the WC content increases to 30%, the WC content is too much, resulting in an excessive amount of the Cr-rich phase being generated in the composite, leading to more prominent interface problems, affecting the bonding between the hard phase and the matrix, resulting in a poor overall lubrication effect and increased friction coefficient of the composite. However, overall, compared with the Cr-rich phase, the distribution of WC particles in the 30 WC–HEA sample is more dispersed, and the effect of WC is more prominent. In this work, WC-FeCoCrNi composites were prepared by the SPS process. The effects of WC content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and wear resistance of WC–HEA composites were studied. The main conclusions are as follows: A single-phase FCC solid solution structure was formed after SPS sintering of the HEA pure matrix powder, which did not appear before sintering, indicating that SPS is helpful for HEA to complete alloying. The sintered WC–HEA composite is mainly composed of an FCC matrix phase (Ni, Fe) and carbide phases (Cr7C3, Co3W3C, WC, etc.). With the increase of WC content, the distribution of WC is dispersed, and the content of Cr7C3 and Co3W3C increases gradually. Some needle-like Cr-rich phases in the FCC matrix coarsen into flakes. Although the addition of WC reduces the densification of the composite to a certain extent, it significantly improves the hardness and compressive yield strength of the matrix. The microhardness of the 30 WC–HEA composite is the highest, at 459.2 HV, which is 71.2% higher than that of the pure matrix material. reading.lever: Introduce an optimal WC content into the HEA to form lubricious carbide phases in situ.
reading.why: This compositional adjustment has demonstrated both friction and wear reduction in related HEA systems and can be tuned for wide temperature stability.
